articles.title: Trump administration proposes changes to Biden-era climate report
articles.summary: The Trump administration is looking to change a portion of a 2023 federal climate report. The administration proposed to reframe how the Fifth National Climate Assessment sees its worst-case scenarios after U.N. scientists said earlier this year that a worst-case scenario was not plausible. In a notice published this week, the Trump administration described the federal climate report’s high-emission scenarios as…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is looking to change a portion of a 2023 federal climate report.

The administration proposed to reframe how the Fifth National Climate Assessment sees its worst-case scenarios after U.N. scientists said earlier this year that a worst-case scenario was not plausible.

In a notice published this week , the Trump administration described the federal climate report’s high-emission scenarios as not representing “plausible policy-relevant baseline futures and should not be used to frame expected, likely, central, or business-as-usual conditions for federal decision making.”

It instructed federal agencies not to treat the worst-case scenario as “expected, likely, baseline, business-as-usual, central, or policy-relevant.”

Last year, the Trump administration also scrubbed the site where the report could be found. However, earlier this year, former employees of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration republished the report on their own website, climate.us .

While it is no longer on a public government website, the report may still be used to inform federal decisionmaking.

Reached for comment, the White House directed The Hill to a Daily Wire article quoting Matthew Wielicki, who directs the U.S. Global Change Research Program, which puts out the report, as saying that “if you look at the last national climate assessment, NCA5, a lot of the impact statements, if not even a majority, in many chapters rely on these now implausible scenarios to kind of inform policymakers about how to respond to climate change.”

Politico reported that Wielicki is a critic of climate science and assumed the role as head of the program earlier this year. Last year, the Trump administration dismissed the scientists working on the next iteration of the report.

The Trump administration’s latest proposal met some pushback.

“This proposed amendment is a clear politicization of climate science,” said Carlos Martinez, senior climate scientist at the Union of Concerned Scientists, in a written statement.

“Dangerous feedback loops, such as the release of methane from melting permafrost, means there is still a significant chance of exceeding 4 degrees Celsius of warming this century, in the range of warming predicted by high-end emission scenarios. Additionally, the latest science suggests that our climate may be more sensitive to emissions than we previously thought, which means that even lower emissions could ultimately induce significant warming similar to that assumed” in the scenarios the Trump administration won’t consider, Martinez added.

In a call with The Hill, Martinez also pointed out that climate scientists also stopped using their best-case climate scenario, saying the Trump administration was not similarly eliminating that consideration.

“It’s very interesting that this amendment is only focusing on the very high-end scenarios and not the low-end scenarios,” he said.

He said that changing the report was “unprecedented” and that the administration should instead make sure the next iteration of the report contains updated information.

articles.title: How an inside ‘scoop’ revealed Pentagon links to pro-Trump influencer
articles.summary: A Utah software engineer, who runs a massive pro-President Trump social media account that has drawn attention from the likes of Elon Musk, made a sinister declaration in a post on Aug. 21. The “Deep State” was setting her up to “commit a crime.” “I have never been more angry in my life,” Jennica Pounds,…
articles.body:
A Utah software engineer, who runs a massive pro-President Trump social media account that has drawn attention from the likes of Elon Musk, made a sinister declaration in a post on Aug. 21.

The “Deep State” was setting her up to “commit a crime.”

“I have never been more angry in my life,” Jennica Pounds, who is behind the DataRepublican account that has nearly 1 million followers on social platform X, wrote in a recent thread.

Over the past week, the resulting saga around Pounds’s allegations has become an obsession of right-wing social media circles, exposed the blurred lines in Pentagon public relations and raised questions about other MAGA-friendly influencers in the military space.

It all started with an offer from a senior State Department official to Pounds. Did she want to publish documents about allegations of censorship under the Biden administration?

“I wanted to give you the option of ‘breaking’ the story as sort of a gift,” Under Secretary of State for Public Diplomacy Sarah Rogers wrote to Pounds.

Pounds initially seemed up for cooperating but later decided the markings on the documents “would have gotten me in big big trouble.”

In a post to her X account, Pounds wrote Friday that “they tried to entrap me” while sharing a screenshot of the text exchange.

Rogers replied to Pounds’s thread that Friday, revealing herself as the official involved.

“lol, these are my text messages and documents. The ‘markings’ are FOIA [Freedom of Information Act] redactions required even for voluntary disclosure. To prove this isn’t a ‘trap,’ I will happily disclose the documents myself,” she wrote, posting the documents in an ensuing thread.

Pounds had earlier concluded the documents “were nothingburgers that did not benefit them at all to release in public.”

Once the exchange went public, the aggregators got to work. Right-wing news aggregator AF Post summarized the back-and-forth between the two women, adding further intrigue by writing that Pounds was an active employee at the Pentagon.

A Pentagon official has since confirmed to The Hill and other news outlets that Pounds is a special government employee at the Defense Department, a work status she did not publicly disclose to her massive online following. It’s unclear if Rogers knew about the job when she offered Pounds the internal documents.

The Hill has reached out to the State Department for comment.

After the revelation, Pounds said her Pentagon press credentials had expired in June, that she did not seek renewal and the next month she began working at the department to “serve the country in a more hands-on way.” She said she would defer questions to Joel Valdez, the Pentagon’s deputy press secretary.

The Defense Department declined to comment when asked about Pounds’s role at the department.

Lauren Harper, the Daniel Ellsberg chair on government secrecy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, told The Hill that Pounds should have disclosed her special government employee status to her followers because otherwise it “blurs the line between journalism and government PR.”

Pounds, too, has championed transparency around potential conflicts of interest.

Late last month, Pounds questioned the alleged friendship between the director of military-leadership blog From the Green Notebook, retired Army Lt. Col. Joe Byerly, and Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, with whom Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has clashed since the start of the Trump administration.

The DataRepublican revelations have raised questions around other prominent accounts that often back the Defense secretary.

Adam D’Ortona, an active-duty Army lieutenant colonel, has openly criticized congressional Democrats, backed Hegseth’s push to root out diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) efforts at the Pentagon and highlighted the Defense secretary’s message of going to war against the department’s bureaucracy.

D’Ortona, who has more than 100,000 followers on X, defended Pounds after it was revealed that she works for the Pentagon, arguing those concerned about the ethics of the incident are like a “burglar lecturing the homeowner about property rights.”

Following the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, USA Today reported in September that D’Ortona works in Hegseth’s office. Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson told the outlet at the time that D’Ortona is not an adviser or spokesperson for the Pentagon.

On Monday, D’Ortona wrote in a response to an X user that “ZERO people are paid” by the Pentagon to “post stories.”

The Army referred questions about D’Ortona to the Pentagon. Hegseth’s office did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

Retired Col. Thomas Anderson, who writes under the pseudonym Cynical Publius, has backed Hegseth’s anti-DEI crusade and has weighed in on a host of political issues, offering his view to more than 320,000 followers on X.

Anderson defended Pounds’s employment at the department in an exchange with journalist Glenn Greenwald.

“I repeat: you do not understand the parameters of being an SGE [special government employee],” Anderson wrote Monday . “It has a specified legal status that she has stayed well within. I’m not your research assistant, I told you what to look up. Go look it up. The truth is never a ‘cliché tactic.’”

When asked Tuesday by The Washington Post Pentagon reporter Dan Lamothe if he also has an SGE status, Anderson did not respond.

articles.title: Letter signed by Democratic senators calls on ICE to halt electric shock gloves
articles.summary: A group of mostly Democratic senators pressed for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to not use gloves that can electrically shock people in a Thursday letter. In the letter addressed to ICE acting Director David Venturella, the senators said they were writing “to express deep concern about U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) plans to…
articles.body:
A group of mostly Democratic senators pressed for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to not use gloves that can electrically shock people in a Thursday letter.

In the letter addressed to ICE acting Director David Venturella, the senators said they were writing “to express deep concern about U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) plans to spend up to $20 million on gloves that deliver electric shocks.”

“Over the past year, ICE personnel have been involved in numerous well-documented incidents of excessive force and civil rights violations. These incidents have shown the American people that ICE personnel are not adequately trained or accountable for their interactions with civilians,” the senators wrote.

The letter was signed by Sens. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.), Angus King (I-Maine), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), Peter Welch (D-Vt.), Patty Murray (D-Wash.), Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.), Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), Jack Reed (D-R.I.), Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.).

Earlier this month , the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) published a notice outlining plans to give ICE officers gloves producing painful electric shocks. The agency was planning to pay up to $20 million for the new devices, also known as the Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter (G.L.O.V.E.), which could be used by officers in the field amid immigration operations.

“ICE is constantly assessing the needs of our officers in the field to ensure they have the tools and equipment necessary to safely arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our country,” a DHS spokesperson previously told NewsNation.

The senators wrote in their letter that “the American people have made it clear that ICE must de-escalate its immigration enforcement operations.”

“ICE must refrain from deployment of the G.L.O.V.E. and instead invest in de-escalation tools, training, and accountability,” they added.

The Hill has reached out to ICE for comment.

articles.title: Investors, Fed watchers want one thing from Kevin Warsh in his Jackson Hole debut: Clarity
articles.summary: The stage is set for Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole speech on Friday.
articles.body:
The stage is set for Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole speech on Friday, offering the new head a chance to clarify the central bank's strategy to bring down inflation and rebuild confidence in the Fed itself.

This year's gathering takes place against a challenging backdrop as inflation remains well above the Fed's 2% goal for the sixth consecutive year after a series of shocks. The latest inflation data offers conflicting evidence , fueling arguments for both patient policymakers who favor holding rates steady and hawks who want to hike rates as soon as possible.

Officials are deeply divided on whether to hold rates steady for now to see if inflation will come down on its own, or to act immediately. This internal tension — the "good family fight" that Warsh desires — resulted in three dissents at the last policy meeting.

The gathering also comes amid a distinct lack of clarity about the Fed's willingness to raise rates. During his July press conference, Warsh repeatedly pointed to bond yields shooting materially higher, suggesting it was a good thing and implying that the Fed welcomes higher yields to tighten policy through markets. His stance initially triggered higher long-term bond yields and ultimately led to confusion and damaged market confidence in the Fed's strategy.

"I would like to hear him explain and start with, 'Here's why we made the decision we made in July,'" Robert Kaplan, former head of the Dallas Fed, told Yahoo Finance.

Kaplan said the Fed chairman doesn't need to predict the future or offer forward guidance. Rather, he needs to "be a faithful reporter of how the committee is working, as opposed to leaving it to people to rely on individual Fed presidents and governors making their own statements.

"I think it would be better if he stepped into that role a little bit more," he continued.

Matt Luzzetti, chief economist for Deutsche Bank, said Warsh's first priority must be a "cleanup" of that July press conference. Luzzetti said unease in the bond markets stems from Warsh's unwillingness to commit to retaining the Personal Consumption Expenditures index as the Fed's favored inflation yardstick, alongside not specifying that rate hikes are the primary method to bring down inflation.

"These ambiguities could be resolved easily at Jackson Hole," Luzzetti said, suggesting either a big-picture talk focused on the Fed's new task forces or a policy-oriented commentary that cleans up recent communication missteps.

articles.title: Trump officials cast doubt on Pennsylvania measles death claims
articles.summary: Top Trump administration health officials are openly questioning the circumstances of two deaths that Pennsylvania officials attributed to measles. “We don’t know exactly what happened in Pennsylvania yet,” Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said in an interview Thursday on Fox Business. “We don’t know if the children died…
articles.body:
Top Trump administration health officials are openly questioning the circumstances of two deaths that Pennsylvania officials attributed to measles.

“We don’t know exactly what happened in Pennsylvania yet,” Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said in an interview Thursday on Fox Business.

“We don’t know if the children died from measles or had another condition that was already attacking them and they happened to get measles at the same time,” Oz said.

Oz was the latest administration official to cast doubt on the accuracy of statements from Pennsylvania authorities, who announced Tuesday two unvaccinated people in Lancaster County died from “measles-associated” conditions.

On Wednesday, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. suggested the deaths might have been completely made up by an aide to Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) to score political points.

“The deaths may even have been altogether fabricated by one of the Governor’s hopeful staffers,” Kennedy wrote on social platform X in part of an escalating online feud touched off by remarks Shapiro made at a Tuesday press conference, where he decried vaccine misinformation coming from the Trump administration and Kennedy specifically.

“Governor Shapiro’s unseemly rush to Lancaster County to convene a national press conference and his giddy delight in announcing two measles deaths was a morose commentary on the contemporary political dialogue,” Kennedy wrote.

During a Wednesday press conference in Tampa, Fla., Kennedy said Shapiro’s office was refusing to provide details to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). He blamed the Biden administration for declining childhood vaccination rates and said the Trump administration was rebuilding trust in the country’s public health authorities.

The official X account of the CDC, meanwhile, doubled down on Kennedy’s skepticism.

“We appreciate Secretary Kennedy’s efforts to clarify conflicting information from Pennsylvania officials about whether the two reported deaths were caused by measles. CDC is working to determine what actually occurred,” the agency said Thursday .

“These discrepancies raise important questions, particularly because the Governor’s Office has not provided CDC with information relevant to the outbreak and has declined our offers of assistance,” the CDC continued.

New CDC Director Erica Schwartz has not made any public remarks about measles since she started the job earlier this month.

The questions from Trump administration officials arose after Shapiro and Pennsylvania Health Secretary Debra Bogen divulged only minimal information during a press conference about the deaths.

Citing patient privacy concerns, Shapiro and Bogen said only that the patients were unvaccinated and from Lancaster County. They did not specify ages or whether they were members of the Amish community or any other religious group that may be more vaccine hesitant.

State officials later said one of the people who died was an infant with a positive measles test. They did not release details about the second person.

Lancaster County Commissioner Josh Parsons (R) said he was not aware of any reported deaths from measles and questioned where the governor got his information.

“As of right now, we have ZERO information that corroborates the idea that there were two measles deaths in Lancaster County,” Parsons wrote on X.

On Thursday, the Lancaster County coroner told local media his office has not confirmed any deaths associated with measles but is reviewing an infant death with a positive measles test.

According to the state health department, the term “measles-associated” is used when “laboratory or epidemiologic evidence of measles is present, but the disease may not be assessed by the medical certifier or coroner to be the immediate cause of death.”

The department also noted that not all deaths are referred to a coroner under Pennsylvania law and just one of the two measles-associated deaths is under investigation by the county coroner.

articles.title: 3 Stars and Stripes staffers sue Pentagon over firings at military news outlet
articles.summary: Three Stars and Stripes staffers sued the Pentagon in federal court Thursday, looking to prevent last week’s firings by the Department of Defense (DOD) at the military-focused newspaper. Stars and Stripes publisher Max Lederer, Editor-in-Chief Erik Slavin and reporter Lara Korte filed the complaint in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, alleging the…
articles.body:
Three Stars and Stripes staffers sued the Pentagon in federal court Thursday, looking to prevent last week’s firings by the Department of Defense (DOD) at the military-focused newspaper.

Stars and Stripes publisher Max Lederer, Editor-in-Chief Erik Slavin and reporter Lara Korte filed the complaint in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, alleging the DOD’s firings of them last Friday are in violation of the department’s own personnel rules and the First Amendment.

“In direct contravention of those First Amendment principles, Defendants are attempting to fire Plaintiffs for speaking up as private citizens in support of the press’s freedom to cover military operations, its need to reach all servicepersons, and in retaliation for their publication of a news report on deteriorating conditions aboard the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln during its extended tour of duty in the Mid-East,” lawyers for Democracy Defenders Fund, Lawyers for Good Government, Government Accountability Project and the Yale Law School Media Freedom and Information Access Clinic — the organizations that filed the lawsuit on behalf of Lederer, Slavin and Korte — wrote in the 45-page complaint.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

Andrew Brey, who is a Pentagon official in Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s office, ordered Lederer to present separation notices to Korte and Slavin on Aug. 12, charging the duo with insubordination for remarks they made during an interview on “CBS Sunday Morning,” according to court documents.

Five days later, Lederer contacted Brey for clarification. Brey told Lederer to “deliver the notices as instructed.” The publisher did not, instead announcing his retirement .

Then, on Aug. 21, all three staffers were fired by the Pentagon in dismissals that are set to take effect in five business days from receiving the memo.

Traditionally, Stars and Stripes has enjoyed editorial independence from the DOD even though its staff are employees of the department. The outlet is partially funded by the Pentagon.

The Pentagon has worked to reshape the editorial coverage of the newspaper, saying it is looking to get rid of “woke distractions” in coverage and refocus it on “warfighting.”

“We will modernize its operations, refocus its content away from woke distractions that syphon morale, and adapt it to serve a new generation of service members,” Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell wrote in January.

The department in April removed Jacqueline Smith, the outlet’s ombudsman, whose role was to monitor the newspaper’s editorial independence and to report concerns to Congress. Smith sued the Pentagon in June over her firing.

The same month, two advisory board members for the Stars and Stripes sued the department , alleging the Pentagon is attempting to censor the newspaper’s content.

The Pentagon put in place Navy Capt. William Urban, an active duty service member, as the new deputy publisher of the newspaper earlier this month, an appointment that triggered questions from Democratic lawmakers.

The same Friday that Lederer, Slavin and Korte were fired, the Pentagon public affairs office released new guidance for the news outlet, stating the paper will maintain “editorial operations independent of the military chain of command, military public affairs activities, or other external influences, free from censorship or propaganda,” but that the newspaper has to “safeguard information by preventing the disclosure of classified information and controlled unclassified information and by avoiding the publication of material that would adversely affect national security or clearly endanger U.S. personnel.”

“Stripes will coordinate all of its congressional briefings, reports and non-newsgathering engagements with the Office of the Assistant Secretary of War for Legislative Affairs (OASW(LA)),” the Pentagon press office wrote in the 17-page document. “Such coordination must occur prior to the engagement and within OASW(LA)-established notification and review timelines.”

The aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt is expected to sail to the Middle East in the coming weeks to relieve another aircraft carrier as the U.S. military in the region continues to enforce the naval blockade in the Arabian Sea.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt and its strike group will depart San Diego and join the other U.S. warships in the U.S. Central Command (Centcom) theater for an over-seven-month deployment to relieve USS George Washington, the USNI News reported .

“ We do these extensions in little chunks , and the families don’t see any endpoint so they can plan their own lives,” Caudle added. “That creates a lot of stress for sailors.”

The USS George Washington, a Nimitz-class carrier, arrived in the Middle East last week, replacing the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose deployment has come under scrutiny over recent news media reports of rough conditions onboard and worsening mental health of some sailors.

articles.summary: The Food and Drug Administration approved updated COVID-19 vaccines on Thursday for people at higher risk, clearing the way for manufacturers to begin shipping them to pharmacies and physicians’ offices. articles.body:
The Food and Drug Administration approved updated COVID-19 vaccines on Thursday for people at higher risk, clearing the way for manufacturers to begin shipping them to pharmacies and physicians’ offices.

The agency greenlit new formulations of the mRNA vaccines from Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna, the companies said. FDA also approved a non-mRNA shot from Sanofi, which was originally licensed to Novavax, according to the company.

The updated shots are meant to better target the currently circulating strains of the virus. The companies said their shots will be available in the coming days.

Coronavirus infections are increasing or likely to be growing in 47 states, according to Aug. 19 data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). But the overall spread of the virus remains low.

Despite the approvals, questions remain about access and affordability to the shots.

Normally, a CDC advisory panel would make recommendations on who is eligible for the vaccine. But a federal court invalidated the appointments of all new members by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., putting the panel in legal limbo.

Insurers typically have to cover most vaccines recommended by the panel. In its absence, there is no such requirement.

Similar to last season, the vaccines were approved for people 65 years and older, as well as younger people with at least one underlying health condition.

The Moderna shot is approved for ages 6 months and older; the Pfizer shot for ages 5 years and older; and the Sanofi shot for ages 12 years and older.

articles.body:
The U.S. military said Thursday that it has cleared all Iranian sea mines along internationally recognized transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz.

In a video posted to the social platform X Thursday evening, U.S. Central Command (Centcom) Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said that “the U.S. military has achieved a major milestone in the Strait of Hormuz.”

“We have successfully cleared sea mines in the strait’s international shipping lanes that were laid months ago by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Internationally recognized transit routes in the strait are free of Iranian sea mines, thanks to the incredible work of the U.S. military,” Cooper added in the video.

If Iranian sea mines have been cleared as Cooper said, vessel movement through the strait will most likely be less restricted.

Traffic in the strait, a key waterway for the oil industry, has been severely restricted during the nearly six-month war against Iran, causing elevated oil and gas prices.

According to AAA , the average price of a regular gallon of gas in the U.S. was about $4.10 late Thursday, up from about $3.21 the year prior

On Monday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent issued a global warning for countries to drop all financial ties with Iran or risk being barred from the U.S. dollar system, kicking off an economic pressure campaign against Tehran.

The campaign, named “Operation Economic Outcast,” has been promoted as a financial “D-Day” akin to the American invasion of Normandy in World War II.

articles.title: Most Asian stocks advance as attention turns to Warsh speech
articles.summary: Asian stocks mostly rose Friday ahead of a closely watched speech by Federal Reserve boss Kevin Warsh that investors will be parsing for clues about the outl...
articles.body:
Asian stocks mostly rose Friday ahead of a closely watched speech by Federal Reserve boss Kevin Warsh that investors will be parsing for clues about the outlook for interest rates amid elevated inflation and no sign of an end to the Middle East crisis.

With the euphoria following Nvidia's blistering earnings report petering out, the attention is back on the economy as debate surrounds if or when the US central bank will tighten monetary policy.

Last month's Fed meeting saw policymakers keep borrowing costs on hold but with three of them dissenting in favour of a hike, and while the latest figures showed inflation easing slightly it remains well above the two percent target.

Worries that price rises will remain elevated for some time -- fuelled largely by a spike in energy costs caused by the Iran war -- have put upward pressure on long-term Treasury yields, making government borrowing increasingly expensive.

Traders are hoping Warsh's speech at the annual meeting of central bankers and economic leaders at Jackson Hole, Wyoming, will give them an insight into decision-makers' thinking.

However, his last major public appearance after the July meeting was widely panned as giving an ambiguous message, and analysts warn that his refusal to give forward guidance will likely mean investors are left disappointed.

Stephen Innes at Quintex Intel said the address -- Warsh's first since taking the helm at the Fed -- was "the most consequential central bank speech left this year", and comes almost three weeks before the next policy announcement.

"Recent data have reduced the immediate need for tighter policy, giving Warsh room to re-establish the Fed's inflation-fighting message without signalling imminent action," he wrote.

"The speech arrives against a difficult policy backdrop. Inflation remains above target for a sixth consecutive year, while Fed officials have begun debating whether tighter policy may still be required."

Asian equity markets were broadly higher in early trade, with tech firms struggling to extend Thursday's rally that came on the back of Nvidia's profit blowout and bumper forecast, which soothed worries over the AI boom.

Tokyo, Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Jakarta and Taipei all rose, though Seoul retreated along with Wellington and Manila.

Wall Street had provided a positive lead, with all three main indexes rising, though the gains were based entirely on the tech sector, which was the only one of 11 to advance.

Oil prices edged down but remain in danger of spiking further as investors await a breakthrough in efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to tanker and cargo traffic.

articles.title: Judge rules Pentagon’s supply chain risk designation for Anthropic was illegal
articles.summary: A federal judge in California ruled on Thursday the Pentagon’s blacklisting of the artificial intelligence firm Anthropic earlier this year was illegal, violating the First Amendment. In a ruling Thursday evening, Judge Rita Lin said the Trump administration retaliated against the Claude-maker for its “constitutionally protected activity,” and violated the Due Process clause of the…
articles.body:
A federal judge in California ruled on Thursday the Pentagon’s blacklisting of the artificial intelligence firm Anthropic earlier this year was illegal, violating the First Amendment.

In a ruling Thursday evening, Judge Rita Lin said the Trump administration retaliated against the Claude-maker for its “constitutionally protected activity,” and violated the Due Process clause of the Fifth Amendment

“Though the Department of War is undisputedly free to select the AI vendor of its choice, the evidence demonstrates that the broad measures imposed on Anthropic were illegal and baseless,” Lin wrote in the 59-page ruling.

Anthropic sued the Trump administration last March, challenging the Pentagon’s decision to label the company a supply chain risk after negotiations fell apart over safety guardrails.

Anthropic demanded its technology to not be used in fully autonomous lethal weapons or for the mass surveillance of Americans, while the Pentagon insisted it be allowed to use Anthropic’s Claude for “all lawful uses.”

In doing so, Pentagon leadership directed offices to cease using Anthropic’s products. Announcing the designation at the time, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said “America’s warfighters will never be held hostage by the ideological whims of Big Tech.”

The AI firm argued in court the Pentagon retaliated against the company over what it believes is a “protected viewpoint” of the company.

Lin agreed, stating Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei was “consistent with a longstanding practice of public speech on AI safety,” when he publicly debated the safety restrictions required for Claude.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) argued speech used within contract negotiations is not protected, but Lin said that position is “unsupported.”

“Defendants claim that because of Anthropic’s ‘increasingly hostile manner through the press’ and its criticism of the Department of War’s views on AI use, defendants ‘cannot trust Anthropic to ensure the integrity of its models,'” Lin wrote.

“Neither the Constitution nor the federal statute invoked by defendants allows them to impose sweeping penalties based principally on Anthropic’s critique of the Administration’s views,” the judge continued.

A spokesperson for Anthropic said the company “welcomed” the ruling.

“We remain focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology,” the spokesperson added.

The DOJ nor Department of Defense immediately responded to request for comment.

While the ruling wraps up Anthropic’s suit in northern California, the company also filed suit over the Trump administration’s actions in Washington, D.C.

A three-judge panel in the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals heard from both sides in May but have not released a decision.

articles.title: Tech firms call for ‘collective action’ against AI-powered hacking
articles.summary: OpenAI leads the call among other technology firms for “collective action” against “AI-enabled cyber attacks.” “Today’s AI advances are already giving defenders new ways to fix weaknesses that have accumulated for years. If we act decisively, we can use the defenders’ window to make our digital world much more secure,” the company wrote in a…
articles.body:
OpenAI leads the call among other technology firms for “collective action” against “AI-enabled cyber attacks.”

“Today’s AI advances are already giving defenders new ways to fix weaknesses that have accumulated for years. If we act decisively, we can use the defenders’ window to make our digital world much more secure,” the company wrote in a letter Thursday .

The letter advised the government to “make cyber defense an immediate leadership priority.”

It also called for coordination among local, national and international governments to “help lead the response to defend against sustained AI-enabled attacks.”

“We call on leaders across industry and government to bring the full weight of their technology, resources, and expertise to this effort,” OpenAI continued in their letter.

Over 100 other tech-related firms signed onto the letter — including Accenture, Anthropic, Cloudflare, Dell, Google, IBM, Microsoft and Palo Alto Networks.

“Together, we can turn today’s AI advances into lasting improvements in security that benefit everyone. Let’s put them to work,” the letter concluded.

It comes a few weeks after OpenAI paused some model training Aug. 18 after its models independently gained access to the internet during testing and hacked into the tech company Hugging Face, who also signed onto the letter.

Anthropic disclosed a similar cybersecurity incident involving Irregular’s misconfiguration. In that case, Anthropic’s Claude model accessed the systems of three organizations.

“This did not involve a sandbox escape or a sophisticated cyber action,” a spokesperson for Irregular told The Hill at the time. “There are no current open issues.”

The incidents worried some Democratic lawmakers who cited the “serious risk that frontier AI models can pose” in separate letters to the top executives at Anthropic and OpenAI earlier this month.

Twenty-nine House Democrats also called for congressional oversight hearings into these cybersecurity incidents, advocating for the implementation of federal guardrails to prevent similar breaches from occurring in the future.

“These are no ordinary cybersecurity incidents,” the lawmakers wrote in a letter to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

A spokesperson for OpenAI told The Hill in a statement that this incident “marked an important moment for AI safety” and said the company will take the lawmakers’ questions “seriously.”

articles.title: Laser used to shoot down cartel drones near Mexico border
articles.summary: The U.S. military this week used a high-energy laser to shoot down three drones near the southern border that officials said were linked to Mexican drug cartels. The operation took place late Tuesday and early Wednesday and involved the Army Multipurpose High Energy Laser system to bring down the drones along the U.S.-Mexican border, Joint…
articles.body:
The U.S. military this week used a high-energy laser to shoot down three drones near the southern border that officials said were linked to Mexican drug cartels .

The operation took place late Tuesday and early Wednesday and involved the Army Multipurpose High Energy Laser system to bring down the drones along the U.S.-Mexican border, Joint Task Force-Southern Border said Thursday.

Officials described the drones, though exact locations were not disclosed, as “hostile” and that they posed a “physical threat” to U.S. service members and Customs and Border Protection personnel.

“Cartel networks are increasingly employing unmanned aircraft systems to facilitate illicit human-smuggling and actively spy on our personnel and law enforcement partners,” said Maj. Gen. Curtis Taylor, who serves as the commander of the border task force, in a statement.

Taylor said the successful takedown of the “adversarial drones” was a “direct testament to the readiness, vigilance, and technological edge.”

“By integrating layered countermeasures alongside advanced directed-energy capabilities like this laser system, we have made it clear that we will not tolerate hostile surveillance,” he added.

Taylor thanked the Mexican government and its military for their cooperation in addressing drone threats in the broader region. It is unclear whether the strikes occurred over U.S. or Mexican territory.

The operation comes as the Trump administration has expanded the military’s role along the southern border as part of President Trump’s immigration crackdown and war on drug cartels.

Roughly 8,000 U.S. service members are currently deployed under Joint Task Force-Southern Border across the nearly 2,000-mile border, according to the military.

Since taking the reins in March 2025, the task force said troops have conducted tens of thousands of detection patrols and observation flights. U.S. forces have also installed hundreds of miles of wire barriers and completed patrols alongside Mexican military personnel.

articles.body:
President Trump announced Friday he would move to allow American farmers and ranchers to process their own food, hitting back against what he called the “monopoly” created by large processors.

Trump noted in a post on Truth Social that farmers and ranchers “have always been a number one priority” for him, adding that he has heard they have had an issue with big processors.

The president wrote, “There are, essentially, 4 of them, a very non competitive number, and they make life miserable for our wonderful Farmers and Ranchers, and I can’t let that happen, can I?”

“So, in order to break this powerful monopoly, with much of its ownership based outside of the U.S., I am authorizing legal documents to be drawn in order to allow Farmers and Ranchers to be given the right to PROCESS THEIR OWN FOOD. This should move quickly,” he continued.

The move comes as Trump has faced backlash from ranchers as well as a number of congressional Republicans after his administration rolled out a plan to import 300,000 metric tons of tariff-free foreign ground beef over 90 days.

The critics argue that selling beef at a 25 percent discount puts downward pressure on what domestic ranches are able to charge. Additionally, industry experts say that savings from the move may not reach shoppers because of large packers and retailers getting the margin.

articles.title: Kevin Warsh didn't bring up the $40 trillion national debt or historic deficits in his Jackson Hole speech
articles.summary: Kevin Warsh didn't directly address eye-popping government debt figures in a speech in Jackson Hole, just days after the gross national debt and bond market...
articles.body:
Kevin Warsh didn't directly address eye-popping government debt figures in his first speech as Federal Reserve chairman at the annual symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyo., on Friday, just days after the gross national debt passed $40 trillion and debt-fueled Treasury bond market jitters spooked investors.

The word "debt" appeared only once in the prepared remarks, at the beginning of Warsh's speech, when he said "everyone here is in debt" to the meeting's hosts.

Warsh did offer in his speech what was perhaps a hint at how he might be hoping the US economy can bring deficits under control, with a bullish assessment that artificial intelligence could mean "the potential for substantially higher growth is on the rise."

"A kind of super Moore's law seems to be playing out," he added, a reference to Gordon Moore, a co-founder of Intel, who once observed that computer processing speed doubles roughly every two years.

That echoed remarks from both Treasury Secretary Bessent and President Trump, who have downplayed the exploding debt by promising that the US can grow its way out of the problem with outsized economic growth that many economists see as unrealistic .

Warsh added that the central bank is watching technology changes attentively, but that a task force on AI he announced earlier this year has yet to offer recommendations, and that those findings will "have no bearing on decisions we make in the current policy conjuncture."

Little focus on government balance sheets

Despite no mention of government balance sheets from Warsh, debt and deficits have been top-of-mind topics for investors , as debt-fueled strains in sovereign bond markets and rising yields have led to economic jitters.

Warsh did make a request in his speech for "clear market signals, as unfiltered as possible," including from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, as to "the prices and trading volumes of Treasury securities."

That mention of Treasurys was also one of the few references to the bond market in Warsh's speech, following weeks of bond market volatility — a major challenge to the US economy, fueled in part by the soaring national debt.

The gross US national debt reached $40.047426 trillion on Aug. 18, hitting that milestone after the government added $1 trillion in new debt in just a few months.

A recent Congressional Budget Office projection also found that the annual US deficit is projected to reach $2.1 trillion by the end of the government's fiscal year on Sept. 30. The US has run debt and deficit levels well above historic norms for years — even when measured against the size of the economy.

articles.title: Officials widen lettuce-linked cyclospora outbreak probe to 20 states
articles.summary: Cases of a parasitic illness linked to iceberg lettuce have been confirmed in 20 states, health officials said, as the largest outbreak of the disease in U.S. history keeps growing. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said Thursday that cyclosporiasis cases have been identified in three additional states:…
articles.body:
Cases of a parasitic illness linked to iceberg lettuce have been confirmed in 20 states, health officials said, as the largest outbreak of the disease in U.S. history keeps growing.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said Thursday that cyclosporiasis cases have been identified in three additional states: Georgia, Tennessee and Texas.

The total number of people sickened by the parasite is now 11,458, up from about 10,900 reported last week.

Epidemiologic data has confirmed that iceberg lettuce sourced from a Taylor Farms central Mexico-based processor was contaminated with the cyclospora parasite and made people sick. Taylor Farms is the world’s largest producer of salads and fresh-cut vegetables.

The affected products have been recalled and the best-by dates have passed. The FDA said it is confident that all recalled ⁠iceberg lettuce has been removed from the market.

Illnesses linked to the outbreak began June 14, and onset dates have continued through Aug. 15, the agencies said.

There have been at least 495 hospitalizations, along with two deaths previously reported in Michigan.

The FDA says its staff remain on-site in Mexico, testing and inspecting lettuce in the fields and the processing facility, in coordination with Mexican officials.

Cyclosporiasis is a foodborne infection caused by a parasite that’s typically spread through food or water contaminated with human feces. Not everyone who is exposed will display symptoms, but the main one is frequent and watery diarrhea.

Outbreaks tend to occur most often in the late spring and summer. Cases are notoriously difficult to track, and sometimes a specific cause is never identified.

The country usually sees a few hundred to a thousand cases at most in a given year. However, the previous worst year in the U.S. for infections was 2019, when about 4,700 illnesses were reported nationally.

articles.body:
The growing backlash against surveillance companies like Flock may have reached a tipping point. A new survey has found that more Americans oppose these surveillance cameras than support them.

According to a new YouGov survey of 20,000 people across the U.S. that was shared exclusively with The Washington Post , 46% of respondents opposed the company’s surveillance cameras in their communities, while 38% supported them. This is a reversal from last year, when the majority of survey respondents said they were in favor.

Flock is one of the more visible surveillance companies, operating more than 120,000 license plate readers across the U.S. that can track the whereabouts of vehicles. The company has been embroiled in controversy following reports of police abusing the cameras’ surveillance , which resulted in dozens of U.S. communities rejecting Flock’s cameras or canceling their contracts amid privacy concerns.

The survey also reported that more respondents said the surveillance would not make them feel any safer.

When reached by TechCrunch, Flock claimed there was wide support for its surveillance technology, but acknowledged that “support isn’t unconditional,” and touted the rollout of its recent safeguards . Critics, like the ACLU, have said the company’s new safeguards amount to little, and Flock remains a major threat to civil liberties.

Amid the intensifying backlash, Flock CEO Garrett Langley last week called for a “compromise” between surveillance and privacy, following a rise in vandalism targeting Flock cameras.

articles.title: Aggressive Treasury yield cap could weigh on dollar, says Citi's asset allocation head
articles.summary: By Mehnaz Yasmin Aug 28 (Reuters) - Aggressive efforts by the U.S.
articles.body:
Aug 28 (Reuters) - Aggressive efforts by the U.S. Treasury to cap long-end borrowing costs below 5.30% could ultimately weigh on the dollar, Citigroup's global head of macro and asset allocation strategy ‌Dirk Willer said, as investors may look beyond Treasuries for assets that offer protection against fiscal deterioration.

Instead, "investors ‌might buy bonds that aren't capped by central banks, creating some negative dollar impetus," Willer told the Reuters Global Markets Forum on Thursday.

Citi had ​been underweight Treasuries but dropped that position after the Treasury announcement, while adding gold and staying short the dollar, he said.

The U.S. Treasury's move last week to support long-duration bonds by doubling buyback sizes did little to alleviate concerns about global duration risk. That further raises interest rate risk, which could help explain why the Treasury "term premium" — the extra compensation investors demand ‌for holding long-maturity debt rather than rolling ⁠over shorter-dated paper — is rising.

A higher term premium pushes up long-term yields, raising borrowing costs across the economy, with the 30-year Treasury serving as a key benchmark for mortgages, corporate borrowing ⁠and other long-term financing.

Burgeoning government debt, as the U.S. runs one of the largest deficits on record, along with elevated inflation and a surge in long-duration debt issuance by AI hyperscalers, have added to pressure on the long end. The 30-year Treasury ​yield soared ​to 5.327% last week, its highest since 2007.

Willer noted that ​it isn't just direct intervention by the Treasury ‌or the Federal Reserve that creates demand for Treasuries. Other measures, such as increasing buybacks, phasing out the 20-year bond, or regulatory changes, could be used to encourage banks or other market participants to increase Treasury holdings.

"In proper bond crises, there are often market-microstructure issues that policymakers can address," he said. "Ultimately the question (is) how many bullets do they have, and when do they run out? We think they still have a fair amount of bullets, while others think they're ‌close to running out."

BOND-OIS CONVERGENCE: THE FISCAL RISK TEST

In the U.S., ​30-year Treasury yields have risen broadly in tandem with matched overnight index ​swap (OIS), leaving the bond-OIS spread relatively contained and ​suggesting the selloff has been driven more by a repricing of rates than Treasury-specific risk.

"If you ‌look at what drove the sell-off, asset-swap spreads ​were quite well behaved. And ​that's really where fiscal problems should show up most clearly," Citi's Willer said.

articles.title: Why are flesh-eating bacteria expanding beyond traditional hotspots?
articles.summary: Scientists have recently documented the bacteria spreading to places that were once too cold for it to survive.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — As water temperatures continue rising , Vibrio, or the dangerous bacteria that can cause a “flesh-eating” disease, may become even more common.

Vibrio naturally occurs in warm, brackish coastal waters. It is especially prevalent in places like Florida, which has the highest case rate, according to the University of Florida . But scientists have recently documented the bacteria spreading to places that were once too cold for it to survive, including as far north as Maine, nonprofit environmental outlet Gist reported .

Vibrio infections “are one of the many incidental potential consequences of a warming climate,” Tobias Dörr, an associate professor of microbiology at Cornell University , said. He explained that while cases remain low, “there is a clear correlation between case load and ocean temperature reported in several studies — case rates tend to be highest in months where the water is the warmest.”

“An increase in water temperature could therefore cause more infections in the future,” Dörr said. “The somewhat good news is that Vibrios did not specifically evolve to live in the human body, and a healthy immune system can in many cases fight off these bacteria.”

Most people become infected by eating raw or undercooked shellfish , particularly oysters, though people can also be exposed when open wounds come into contact with contaminated water, according to the Florida Department of Health .

About 80,000 people get vibriosis every year, with 52,000 resulting from eating contaminated food, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Most cases aren’t life-threatening, but some people may also contract a more severe strain of the bacterium, Vibrio vulnificus.

Vibrio vulnificus can cause necrotizing fasciitis , a serious bacterial infection commonly referred to as “flesh-eating” disease. About 1 in 5 people die from the infection, sometimes within 48 hours. Officials in Florida and Louisiana have reported at least eight Vibrio-related deaths this year.

Nexstar’s Alix Martichoux contributed to this report.

In a Truth Social post, Trump quoted Interior’s Greg Wischer as saying, “I visited the Reflecting Pool this morning, and pictures are included below…
articles.body:
President Trump posted an update Friday on the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, quoting an Interior Department official as saying it was “Coming out great!” and will be open in a few weeks.

In a Truth Social post , Trump quoted Interior’s Greg Wischer as saying, “I visited the Reflecting Pool this morning, and pictures are included below of the pool reflecting and the American Flag Blue color.”

The post, entirely attributed to Wischer, also said the pool will “be opening in a few weeks. Will be a beauty. NO VANDALS PLEASE.”

It also said it has been partially refilled so that National Park Service staff and contractors can flush its piping system.

The state of the Reflecting Pool has been a source of controversy in recent weeks. The president repeatedly touted the multimillion-dollar project while it was underway, but it appeared to be gray and peeling after its expected completion date.

The unusual use of no-bid contracts for work on the Reflecting Pool has been a particular source of scrutiny.

Trump and the Interior Department have blamed vandals for the state of the pool. However, a recent filing from U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro cast doubt on that narrative and instead blamed botched work.

Trump’s latest post blamed previous administrations, saying, “After years of neglect by previous administrations, more than half of the 58 water supply ports were so clogged that they were deemed nonfunctioning. This work is ongoing. We waited until after July 4th to do. Coming out great!”

articles.title: Chinese hackers target NASA and key US agencies, DOJ alleges
articles.summary: The FBI and Justice Department seized domains tied to QScan and QTRouter, tools allegedly used by China-linked hackers to breach NASA and other agencies.
articles.body: Some cyberattacks start with a suspicious email. Others begin somewhere you would probably never think to look. It could be an old router in someone's home. Maybe it is a forgotten security camera that still connects to the internet. Hackers can compromise vulnerable connected devices and use them to disguise where an attack really comes from. That tactic played a role in a China-linked hacking operation that U.S. authorities say took aim at some of America's most sensitive networks. On Aug. 26, the Justice Department and FBI confirmed intrusion attempts since 2018 against NASA, the Federal Reserve, the Justice Department and the U.S. Senate. Other targets included the Department of Energy, Department of Health and Human Services and National Institutes of Health. FBI WRAPS UP CYBERCRIME OPERATION TARGETING GLOBAL NETWORKS PREYING ON AMERICANS Four unnamed companies in the United States and South Korea were reportedly targeted as well. The names behind the operation sound like something from an IT department: QScan and QTRouter. Yet what these tools allegedly did should get your attention. Here is how the hacking operation worked, how authorities shut it down and what you can do to keep your own connected devices from becoming part of an attacker's network. THIS SATURDAY! Free live CyberGuy class: Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward. Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com. Chinese hackers breached NASA and other U.S. targets According to the Justice Department, a Chinese state-sponsored group known as QTFY created and operated QScan and QTRouter. Federal officials say the group worked for China-based Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology Company. The Justice Department alleges that the company offered hacking services to paying customers, including China's Ministry of State Security and People's Liberation Army. Authorities say QTFY infrastructure has been used to compromise critical infrastructure and other sensitive networks since at least 2018. Court documents also describe targets that included hospitals, telecommunications providers, financial institutions and defense contractors. CyberGuy reached out to NASA about the Justice Department's announcement. "NASA is committed to the cybersecurity and the protection of our systems," NASA spokesperson Jennifer Dooren said. "We work closely with our federal partners, including the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, to quickly address identified vulnerabilities. We continuously collaborate with software partners and actively monitor and assess our networks, software, and data for potential risks. "For security reasons, NASA does not comment on specific reports of potential vulnerabilities or incidents. For additional information regarding this matter, please contact the Department of Justice." We also reached out to the Chinese Embassy in Washington about the Justice Department's allegations. "I am not aware of the specifics you mentioned," an embassy spokesperson told CyberGuy. "China is a firm defender of cybersecurity. The Chinese government firmly opposes and combats all forms of cyberattacks in accordance with the law. We urge the U.S. side to stop using cybersecurity issues to smear or discredit China. "China firmly opposes the U.S. overstretching the concept of national security and using it as a pretext to impose discriminatory restrictions on Chinese companies and will firmly safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies." After we sent the embassy the specific Justice Department release outlining the allegations involving QScan and QTRouter, the embassy told CyberGuy it had "no further information to add at the moment." China has repeatedly denied accusations that it sponsors malicious cyber activity. What stands out here is the infrastructure behind the attacks. Federal investigators describe a system designed to find vulnerable devices and then use some of those devices to help hide malicious activity. How QScan and QTRouter worked QScan handled the hunting. The Justice Department says the platform scanned for vulnerable systems and automatically infected thousands of internet-of-things devices around the world. Those compromised devices could then become part of QTRouter. QTRouter served as what investigators call an obfuscation network. In everyday language, it helped conceal where an attack really came from. The network included compromised IoT devices along with commercial proxy devices and leased virtual private servers. Attackers could route malicious communications through that infrastructure. As a result, the activity could appear to originate outside China or even near the network being targeted. That creates a serious challenge for security teams trying to track an attacker. Think about all the internet-connected equipment people rarely touch after setting it up. A router might sit in the corner for years. A security camera could keep running long after its manufacturer stops releasing updates. Hackers pay attention to forgotten devices because those devices can give them somewhere to hide. FBI Director Kash Patel emphasized how the infrastructure helped conceal the attackers. "These tools were used by PRC cyber actors to hide the origin of their attacks," Patel said. TRUMP PLAN TAPS US FIRMS TO FIGHT FOREIGN CYBERCRIME Why your connected devices enter the picture You were probably nowhere near the hackers' list of targets. NASA and the Federal Reserve operate in a very different security world from your living room. However, the infrastructure behind these attacks creates a connection to everyday technology. QScan allegedly infected IoT devices and pulled them into a larger network. Those compromised devices then helped disguise malicious traffic. So an insecure connected device can become useful to an attacker even when the attacker has little interest in its owner. You may never see a ransom note. Your smart device could continue working normally. Yet vulnerable equipment can potentially provide infrastructure for malicious activity happening somewhere else. That is one reason I keep telling you to pay attention to the router sitting behind the couch. How federal agents pulled the plug The Justice Department obtained court authorization to seize domains used by QScan and QTRouter. Those domains turned out to be a critical weakness. Federal officials say the domains were hard-coded into the malware and used for essential functions, including communication and authentication. Once authorities seized them, the Justice Department says QScan and QTRouter became inoperable. Investigators went after infrastructure that the hacking platforms needed to work. Black Lotus Labs says targeting shared infrastructure like this can damage more than one cyber operation at a time. Its researchers wrote that "taking down a single quartermaster's obfuscation network systematically degrades the capabilities of multiple active threat campaigns at once." Black Lotus Labs also says it shared threat intelligence with U.S. government agencies about emerging risks and null-routed traffic to known infrastructure used by the operators. The researchers describe the operation as a kind of cyber "quartermaster," providing shared reconnaissance, routing and concealment infrastructure that multiple China-linked threat actors could use. That approach has become a recurring part of the U.S. response to China-linked cyber operations. This follows years of China-linked hacking warnings The latest operation follows several previous federal efforts targeting Chinese hacking groups. In 2025, the FBI removed PlugX surveillance malware from more than 4,000 U.S. computers infected by the China-sponsored Mustang Panda group. In 2024, federal agents disabled a botnet made up of hundreds of thousands of infected IoT devices associated with Flax Typhoon. The FBI previously disrupted another botnet used by Volt Typhoon to conceal attacks targeting U.S. and foreign critical infrastructure. CyberGuy has also reported on Salt Typhoon, the China-linked hacking campaign that penetrated major American telecommunications networks. These operations work differently. However, they show how valuable compromised infrastructure can become for state-backed hackers. How to protect your router and connected devices You cannot personally stop a nation-state hacking operation. However, you can make your own devices much harder for attackers to compromise or use as part of their infrastructure. 1) Update your router firmware Your router runs software called firmware, and security fixes are often delivered through firmware updates. Open your router's app or administration page and check for updates. If your router supports automatic updates, turn them on. 2) Replace a router that no longer gets security updates An old router can keep working long after the manufacturer stops protecting it. Check your router's model number on the manufacturer's website to see whether it still receives firmware and security updates. If it has reached end of its life, replace it with a supported model. The FBI has previously warned that cybercriminals actively exploit aging routers that no longer receive security patches. 3) Change your router's administrator password Do not leave the router's administrator account using its original or default password. Create a long, strong and unique password that you have never used for another account. A password manager can help you generate and securely store it. If your router offers two-factor authentication (2FA) for administrator access, turn it on. 4) Use a strong Wi-Fi password Your Wi-Fi network should also have its own strong, unique password. Avoid names, addresses, phone numbers or other information someone could easily guess. Do not reuse the password you use to administer the router. 5) Use WPA3 encryption when available Check your router's wireless security settings. WPA3-Personal offers stronger protection and should be your first choice when your router and devices support it. If WPA3 causes compatibility problems with older devices, use WPA2-Personal with AES or a WPA2/WPA3 compatibility mode. Avoid older WEP and WPA security. 6) Turn off remote administration Most people have no reason to change their router settings while away from home. Look for a setting called Remote Management, Remote Administration or WAN Access. Disable it unless you specifically need it. The FBI has specifically warned that exposed remote administration can give attackers another way to target vulnerable routers. 7) Disable WPS and unnecessary UPnP access Wi-Fi Protected Setup, or WPS, can make connecting devices easier. However, most people do not need to leave it enabled after setup. Also check Universal Plug and Play, or UPnP. It allows devices to automatically request network access and open connections through your router. If none of your devices require it, turning UPnP off can reduce unnecessary exposure. 8) Make sure your router's firewall is turned on Most routers include a built-in firewall. Check your router settings and make sure the firewall remains enabled. Avoid changing advanced firewall settings unless you understand what they control. 9) Put smart devices on a separate network If your router supports a guest network or dedicated IoT network, consider putting security cameras, smart plugs, speakers and other connected gadgets there. Separating those devices from the laptops and phones where you keep sensitive information can limit an attacker's reach if one smart device gets compromised. 10) Update your smart-home devices too Your router is only one piece of the network. Check security cameras, doorbells, smart TVs and other connected devices for software or firmware updates. Enable automatic updates when available. If a smart device has reached the end of its support life and no longer receives security fixes, consider replacing it. 11) Change default passwords on connected devices Some cameras, smart-home hubs and other IoT gear come with preset administrator credentials. Change those passwords during setup. Use a unique password for each important device or account. 12) Review everything connected to your Wi-Fi Open your router's app or administration page and look at its list of connected devices. Make sure you recognize what is there. If you see a device you cannot identify, investigate it. Change your Wi-Fi password if necessary and reconnect only the devices you trust. 13) Remove connected devices you no longer use An old security camera in the garage or smart plug sitting in a drawer can still be connected to your network. Remove devices you no longer use from your Wi-Fi. Disconnect or reset the hardware before getting rid of it. 14) Keep computers and phones updated and protected Install operating system and security updates on your computers, phones and tablets as soon as practical. Strong antivirus software can also help detect malware, malicious downloads and dangerous links before they create another route into your devices. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 15) Know the signs of a compromised router Unexpected settings changes, unfamiliar devices appearing on your network, repeated connectivity problems or unusual router behavior deserve attention. If something looks wrong, reboot the router and check its settings for changes you did not make. If suspicious activity continues, contact your internet provider or router manufacturer. You may need to factory-reset the router and set it up again using trusted settings. Kurt's key takeaways What catches my attention here is how much effort went into hiding the origin of these attacks. The hackers allegedly built infrastructure that could scan for vulnerable devices, compromise them and then use those devices as cover. Federal agents eventually found a pressure point by seizing domains the malware needed to operate. That is a significant win. Still, one disruption leaves a much larger cyber fight in place. State-backed groups keep looking for vulnerable infrastructure because forgotten connected devices are everywhere. Your router may seem like nothing more than the box keeping Netflix running and your phone online. To an attacker, an unpatched device can have an entirely different purpose. For you, the lesson is surprisingly practical. That router you have ignored for five years deserves a checkup. The same goes for old smart-home gear that still connects to the internet. If a manufacturer stopped protecting a device, think carefully about whether you want to keep giving it access to your network.
